_comment: The verdict trace, as a specification rather than as whatever the backend
happened to emit this week.
This exists for the reason testdata/rule_corpus.jsonl exists, and it is
deliberately in the same place. Two implementations of one shape drift, and
nobody finds out until a reader is shown a field that is not there. The
trace already has two implementations - backend/app/services/trace.py
produces it and frontend/src/lib/scanResult.ts consumes it - and nothing
has been holding them together.
It has moved three times already: model.cached and first_judged_at in #68,
provenance in #79, retrieval in #94. Each of those needed a matching edit
in the TypeScript, and each of them got one because the same person made
both. That is not a mechanism.
A third implementation is coming. #83 wants the Android client to produce a
trace mirroring this one so support can compare what the phone decided
against what the server would have said. Writing the contract before that
exists is the cheap moment; rule parity had to be retrofitted after the
second engine already disagreed.
CHECKED BY: backend/tests/test_trace_schema.py, which asserts both that the
backend emits what is described here and that the TypeScript declares it.
Neither direction is optional - a field the backend sends and the client
does not know about is invisible evidence, and a field the client renders
and the backend never sends is a permanently empty panel.

rule_review.why: Whether a speaker of this language has read its detection rules. REVIEW_STATUS existed only in the benchmark payload, which no user sees, so someone scanning in one of the eight unreviewed languages had no way to know how much to trust the verdict in front of them.

properties.native_reviewed: boolean — a speaker has read the native-script rules
properties.code_mixed_reviewed: boolean — always true. Every language falls back to the English rules, which are reviewed, so a code-mixed message is caught by reviewed rules in all twelve. Split from native_reviewed because reporting one boolean would overstate the gap as badly as reporting nothing understates it.
properties.inherited_from: string | null — mr borrows Hindi's rules because the vocabulary genuinely overlaps. Weaker than review, stronger than nothing, and its own claim.
properties.reviewed_via: string | null — the language a reviewed-by-proxy review went through. Separate from inherited_from because the two answer questions about different objects: inherited_from says whose rules these are, reviewed_via says who read them and through what. Marathi inheriting Hindi's rules involves no human at all. A language code, never a reviewer's name — the name is unnecessary for the claim and would be personal data in a payload handed to every client.

offline_rules_fired.why: Always present, empty when nothing fired. An absent key and an empty list would be read as the same thing by a UI and they are not: 'no rule matched' is a statement about the message.

retrieved_patterns.why: Always present. Empty means either that this language has no corpus or that nothing was close, which is exactly why `retrieval` below exists - the list alone cannot say which.

retrieval.why: Whether there was a corpus to ground the verdict in at all (#88). Nine of twelve languages have none, and without this a verdict there is indistinguishable from a grounded one.

language_covered.why: null is a third state, not a falsy second. A cache hit skips retrieval, so coverage was never established - reporting false would assert a gap on a scan that did not look.

patterns_used.why: How many cleared the weak-match floor and reached the prompt. Not derivable from patterns_retrieved: five retrieved with none used is a different verdict from five used.

skipped.why: Present only when retrieval did not run, naming the reason. Today the only value is 'cache_hit'.

model.why: Absent on the degraded path, where both providers were down and the offline rules alone produced the verdict. There is no model to stamp, and inventing one would credit a call that never happened.

cached.why: Present only on a cache hit. Without it the audit record credits a model call that did not happen, and two identical verdicts cannot be told apart from two independent judgements.

link_signals.why: Absent when the message contained no link — most SMS does not, and an empty object would read as 'the links were checked and were fine'. A2 stage 1's named signals, carried into the trace because §01 blocks on two independent signals with at least one deterministic, and the person a block affects has to be able to see which two and why either counted. A blended score here would make an appeal unanswerable.

signals.why: One entry per named check that fired. Never a total: the policy counts signals, and a sum cannot be taken apart again into which ones agreed.

independent_witnesses.why: Distinct bases, NEVER the length of `signals`. Three checks reading one host label are one witness — homograph, lookalike and suspicious-TLD all fire on a single Cyrillic-spelled domain, and counting those as three would auto-block every user on one observation about one string.

deterministic_witness.why: Whether at least one signal is immune to page content. The Confirmed tier requires it, and a model that has just read attacker-controlled text cannot be the sole witness to its own conclusion.

verdict_floor_applied.why: Whether the link evidence stopped a `safe` verdict standing. Link signals are evidence rather than the verdict, so they never override it — but a `safe` verdict displayed above independent bases saying the link is phishing is confidently wrong, and the user reads the verdict rather than reconciling it against the trace. A floor only ever raises caution: `suspicious` and `high_risk` are untouched, and it applies on the cached path too so a domain blocklisted since the message was first judged can only make a stale verdict more cautious.

items.name: string
items.basis: string — which observation it derives from; two signals sharing one are one witness
items.detail: string — the finding in words a user can act on

sender.why: Email only. Absent for SMS and pasted text, which have no sender to check, and absent rather than a null verification because 'this channel has no sender' and 'this sender could not be checked' are different statements.

verification.why: pass | fail | unverifiable. `unverifiable` is the NORMAL case, not the exception: share-to-app delivers text/plain, and SPF needs the connecting IP while DKIM needs raw bytes that sharing rewrites. A `pass` adds no evidence in either direction — it says the message really came from the domain it claims, never that the domain is trustworthy, and compromised-account phishing authenticates perfectly.

caveats.why: User-facing statements that are NEVER counted as evidence. 'We could not verify the sender' has to reach the user and must not reach the blocking policy — if it did, every forwarded email would carry a free witness toward being blocked, which is absence of evidence promoted into evidence on this feature's most common input.

audit.why: Absent when the audit write failed. That is deliberate and load-bearing: a user mid-scam gets their warning even when the compliance record cannot be written, and the response says so by omitting this rather than by faking a record. See ARCHITECTURE.md #05.

_adding_a_field: 1. Add it here first, with a `why`. If you cannot write the why, the field
probably belongs in a log rather than in a trace a bank reads.
2. Run backend/tests/test_trace_schema.py. It should now fail in both
directions - if it does not, the test is not checking what you think.
3. Emit it from trace.py and declare it in scanResult.ts.
4. Optional or required is a real decision, not a default. Optional means
'a legitimate verdict can lack this', and the `why` has to say when.
